newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia embraces Iran despite West's anger.
newsitem.headline: Russia embraces Iran despite West's anger.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin offered on Friday to strengthen Russia's ties with Iran, which faces fresh diplomatic rebuffs from the West after a German court concluded that Tehran's top leaders were responsible for state terrorism.
Yeltsin, speaking to visiting Iranian parliament head Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, said there were reasons "to strengthen and develop... relations" between the two countries.
"We have good, positive co-operation with Iran, which shows a tendency to grow," a smiling Yeltsin told the white-bearded, turbaned Iranian.

Russia has been seeking to diversify its foreign policy partners at a time when Western Europe is ignoring Moscow's protests and going ahead with plans to expand the NATO alliance into eastern Europe.
Yeltsin's public calls for closer ties with Iran put him decidedly out of step with Western countries including the United States, which calls Iran a sponsor of international terrorism.

Germany, Russia's biggest Western trading partner, expelled four Iranian diplomats on Thursday after a Berlin court announced its conclusion that Iran had ordered the 1992 murders of Kurdish activists in Berlin.
The European Union, which Moscow said last month it wanted to join, suggested after the verdict that member countries recall their ambassadors from Iran "for consultations".
Nateq-Nouri's visit also illustrates the changing priorities in Russian foreign policy.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, a Middle East specialist appointed last year, has made better relations with this region and the rest of Asia a policy priority.

Moscow announced on Thursday it would host Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this month for a visit designed to build the foundations for closer ties after decades of mutual distrust following border clashes in the 1960s.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda visited Moscow last month.
Russia also sees considerable commercial and diplomatic opportunity in Iran, and is building a nuclear power plant there despite strong U.S. objections.
Nateq-Nouri, addressing the Russian parliament in Farsi, hailed improving relations between Moscow and Tehran and said their geographical closeness gave them common interests.
"We are sure that Iranian-Russian relations are based on a firm foundation, long-term perspective and unchanging interests," he said, in remarks released in Russian translation.
He did not refer to the German court ruling.

The court said a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, its religious leader, intelligence minister and the head of foreign policy had ordered the assassination of four Kurdish Iranian leaders in 1992.
Nateq-Nouri also attacked Western countries in his remarks to parliament, which is dominated by communists and their conservative allies.
"Some expansionist Western countries, under the pretext of fundamental changes in Russia, are trying to impose on the world a certain type of guardianship," Nateq-Nouri said.
"And we have common official opinion of this issue, which is the world community does not need any kind of guardianship."
